title: Encapsulation & abstraction
griotIntro: The baobab pod protects its seeds inside a solid shell — you use the fruit without needing to know each seed.
Encapsulation hides an object's internal details; abstraction exposes only what's essential for using it.

explanation.text: Encapsulation protects an object's internal data; abstraction exposes a simple interface while hiding the complexity. Click on the lines to see how this bank account protects its balance.

annotations.note: `#balance` is private: no outside code can do `account.#balance = 1000000` directly — that's encapsulation.
We protect the invariant "the balance can't become invalid because of a negative deposit" right at the entry of the method.
Only this method, inside the class, is allowed to modify `#balance`.
`get balance()` exposes a simple read interface, without ever revealing how the data is stored internally — that's abstraction.

useCases: This project's `PrismaClient` (`backend/src/db/prisma.js`) hides all the complexity of connecting to PostgreSQL behind a simple API (`.user.create()`, `.user.findUnique()`).
A `WavePayment` class that only exposes `pay(amount)`, hiding the details of calling Wave's external API.
A React component that only exposes its props, hiding its internal state and rendering logic from the rest of the application.

relatedTools.name: TypeScript (private / #private)
relatedTools.description: Reinforces encapsulation at compile time, on top of modern JavaScript's native private fields (`#field`).

relatedTools.name: Interfaces (TypeScript, Java)
relatedTools.description: Define a public contract without revealing the implementation — abstraction formalized in the type system.

relatedTools.name: Public APIs of libraries (e.g. Prisma)
relatedTools.description: Deliberately expose few public methods while hiding a complex internal implementation.

bugHunt.explanation: The `balance` property is public and can be modified directly without going through `deposit()`, which makes it possible to break the invariant (like a negative balance). It should be private (`#balance`) with controlled access.

practice.question: Why make a property private (`#balance`) rather than public in a class?
options: To prevent any direct modification that would bypass business rules (e.g. a negative balance)
So the code runs faster
It has no real benefit

feedback.correct: Correct — encapsulation protects the object's invariants (here, preventing an inconsistent balance).
feedback.incorrect: Private visibility has no impact on speed; it protects the integrity of internal data.

quiz.question: What is the difference between encapsulation and abstraction?
options: Encapsulation hides implementation details; abstraction defines a simplified interface for the class's user
It's the opposite: abstraction hides the details, encapsulation defines the interface
Abstraction only concerns databases

quiz.question: Why prefer a getter over direct access to a private property?
options: It allows controlling/validating access, and changing the internal implementation without breaking calling code
A getter is always faster than direct access
It's never recommended

quiz.question: An interface (or abstract class) mainly allows you to:
options: Define a contract that concrete classes must follow, without imposing the implementation
Store data in a database
Completely replace tests

quiz.question: What is the risk if all of a class's properties are public?
options: Any external code can modify the object's state and break its internal invariants
The code automatically becomes faster
There is no risk

quiz.question: In an interview, how would you illustrate abstraction with a simple example?
options: "When I drive a car, I don't need to understand the engine to press the accelerator"
"Abstraction is just making a variable global"
"Abstraction has no possible concrete example"

quiz.question: What happens if a class exposes a public setter with no validation on a property that's supposed to be encapsulated?
options: It recreates a breach in encapsulation, allowing business rules to be bypassed as if the property were public
Nothing, a setter is always safe by definition
It automatically improves performance

quiz.question: In TypeScript, a public method that does `return this.#items;` (returns a direct reference to a private array) violates which principle?
options: Encapsulation, because the caller can directly mutate the internal array (`.push()`) without going through the intended methods, even though the property looks protected
The single responsibility principle, and only that one
No principle: returning a reference is always safe

culture: Modern languages diverge culturally on strict encapsulation: Java/C# enforce it by convention (private/public), while Python has no true encapsulation (just a _name convention) — a deliberate choice ("we're all consenting adults").

pionnier.portrait: Two Norwegian computer scientists who designed the Simula language at the Norwegian Computing Center in Oslo in the 1960s.
pionnier.contribution: They created Simula 67, the first language to introduce the notions of class and object, laying the conceptual groundwork for object-oriented programming.
pionnier.problematique: Modeling complex simulation systems (queues, industrial processes) where existing procedural languages became unmanageable as complexity grew.
pionnier.solution: Group related data and behaviors into instantiable "classes" turned into "objects", each encapsulating its own internal state.
pionnier.resultat: Simula directly inspired Smalltalk, C++, and nearly all modern object-oriented languages; Dahl and Nygaard received the Turing Award in 2001 for this contribution.

ambiguite.question: Is a private field (#balance) in JavaScript really impossible to bypass?
ambiguite.reponse: Yes, unlike the _balance convention (just a convention, easily bypassed): modern JavaScript's (ES2022) #private fields are genuinely inaccessible from outside the class, enforced by the JS engine itself.

title: Inheritance & polymorphism
griotIntro: A child inherits traits from their family, but each expresses those traits in their own way.
Inheritance shares common behavior between classes; polymorphism lets each one express it differently.

explanation.text: Inheritance lets a child class reuse the behavior of a parent class; polymorphism lets you call the same method on different objects, each responding in its own way. Click on the lines to see both at work.

annotations.note: `extends Animal`: `Dog` inherits everything `Animal` has, without having to rewrite it.
`Dog` redefines ("overrides") `speak()` with its own behavior — it replaces `Animal`'s version for this class.
Its own version of `speak()`, different from `Dog`'s.
The same call `a.speak()` on each object, but different behavior depending on the actual class of `a` — that's polymorphism.

useCases: Different payment methods (`CardPayment`, `WavePayment`, `CashPayment`) that all inherit from a `Payment` class and implement `pay()` differently.
A notification hierarchy (`EmailNotification`, `SmsNotification`) that share common behavior but express it differently.
The browser DOM: `HTMLButtonElement` and `HTMLInputElement` both inherit from `HTMLElement` and share its base methods.

relatedTools.name: Java / C# / PHP (classic OOP)
relatedTools.description: Languages where class inheritance is central and heavily used in enterprise frameworks.

relatedTools.name: JavaScript (class extends)
relatedTools.description: Implements prototype-based inheritance under a modern class syntax, since ES6.

relatedTools.name: Browser DOM
relatedTools.description: The whole hierarchy of HTML elements (`HTMLButtonElement`, `HTMLInputElement`...) is a native, massive example of inheritance.

lines: constructor(width, height) { this.width = width; this.height = height; }
function testArea(rect) { rect.width = 5; rect.height = 4; return rect.area() === 20; }
bugHunt.explanation: `testArea` assumes `width` and `height` can be modified independently for any `Rectangle`, which is true for a `Rectangle` but false for a `Square` (where width must always equal height): called with a `Square`, the function gives an inconsistent result because `Square` violates the Liskov substitution principle — a subclass should never change the expected behavior of its parent class.

practice.question: What does polymorphism enable in the example above?
options: Calling `speak()` on objects of different classes, each running its own implementation
Preventing any method redefinition
Merging the Dog and Cat classes into one

feedback.correct: Correct — same call, different behavior depending on the object's actual type.
feedback.incorrect: Polymorphism is exactly the possibility of the same method call producing different behaviors.

quiz.question: Why can inheritance become a trap when overused?
options: It creates tight coupling between parent and child classes, making the code rigid in the face of change
Inheritance never has any downsides
It always makes the code faster

quiz.question: What is "duck typing" (used in JS/Python), related to polymorphism?
options: If an object has the expected method/behavior, you can use it without checking its exact class
A mandatory strict typing technique
A pattern reserved for databases

quiz.question: What does "override" (method redefinition) mean in inheritance?
options: A child class provides its own implementation of a method already defined in the parent class
Deleting a method from the parent class
Creating a new class unrelated to the parent

quiz.question: The Liskov substitution principle (the "L" in SOLID) is directly related to:
options: Inheritance: a subclass should be able to replace its parent class without changing the expected behavior
Database management only
The Singleton pattern

quiz.question: What is a classic example where inheritance is misused?
options: `Square extends Rectangle` when changing a Square's width must also change its height, which violates the Rectangle's expected behavior
A `Dog extends Animal` class that redefines `speak()`
There is no such thing as misuse of inheritance

quiz.question: What is an "abstract" method in a parent class?
options: A method declared but without implementation in the parent class, which every child class must implement
A method that can never be called
A method that is automatically private

quiz.question: A `Bird` class has a `fly()` method. A `Penguin extends Bird` class redefines `fly()` to throw an exception "I don't fly". What's the problem?
options: It violates the Liskov substitution principle: a `Penguin` cannot be used everywhere a `Bird` is expected without breaking the behavior
No problem, it's a normal method redefinition
The problem is purely a performance issue

culture: "Favor composition over inheritance" has become a dominant cultural mantra in the industry since the 2000s, in reaction to the abuses of deep inheritance in the 90s (6-7-level class hierarchies that became unmanageable).

pionnier.portrait: American computer scientist, researcher at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, who coined the term "object-oriented programming".
pionnier.contribution: He designed Smalltalk, one of the very first fully object-oriented languages, drawing inspiration from Simula's classes.
pionnier.problematique: Creating a software system where autonomous units could collaborate by simply sending messages, rather than through direct manipulation of shared data.
pionnier.solution: A model where absolutely everything is an object, each object holding its own state and communicating with others solely through sending messages (method calls).
pionnier.resultat: Smalltalk introduced concepts still central today (windows, mouse-driven graphical interface) and directly influenced Objective-C, Java, Ruby, and the modern design of inheritance and polymorphism.

ambiguite.question: Does polymorphism necessarily require inheritance?
ambiguite.reponse: No: in JavaScript/Python (dynamic typing), "duck typing" allows polymorphism with no inheritance relationship at all — if an object has the expected method, it can be used, regardless of its class.

title: Composition vs inheritance
griotIntro: A good craftsman assembles independent pieces to build a flexible object, rather than carving a single block that's impossible to modify.
"Favor composition over inheritance" is one of the most repeated pieces of advice in modern object-oriented design.

explanation.text: Composition builds an object by giving it other objects as dependencies ("has-a"), rather than through inheritance ("is-a") — more flexible at runtime. Click on the lines to compare the two approaches.

annotations.note: With inheritance, every new flying behavior requires a new subclass hard-coded into the codebase — rigid to evolve.
The flying behavior is injected from outside, as a constructor parameter — this is the "has-a" relationship (the duck HAS a flying behavior).
`fly()` simply delegates to whatever behavior was injected.
You can give any flying behavior at runtime, without creating a new class or touching `Duck`.

useCases: This project's React hooks (`useProgress`, `useAuth`) compose reusable behaviors into a component, without any class hierarchy.
An Express middleware injected into a route (`requireAuth`) rather than a `ProtectedRoute` class inheriting from a `Route` class.
A notification service that receives its sending strategy (email, SMS, push) as a parameter instead of inheriting from a specific class.

relatedTools.name: React Hooks
relatedTools.description: `useProgress`, `useAuth` (this project) compose reusable behaviors without a class hierarchy — the most visible example of composition in React.

relatedTools.name: Dependency Injection (NestJS, Spring)
relatedTools.description: Injects dependencies (services) into an object rather than having it inherit them, favoring composition.

relatedTools.name: Express middlewares
relatedTools.description: Assembled together (`app.use(middleware1, middleware2)`) rather than forming a class hierarchy.

bugHunt.explanation: With composition, injecting the same shared instance (`sharedLogger`) into several objects creates hidden coupling: modifying `serviceA.logger.prefix` also affects `serviceB.logger`, since it's the same object in memory. For safe composition, either create a new `Logger` instance per service, or make the injected behavior immutable.

practice.question: What is the main advantage of composition over inheritance?
options: It allows changing a behavior at runtime without depending on a rigid class hierarchy
It makes the code impossible to test
It's always slower than inheritance

feedback.correct: Correct — runtime flexibility, low coupling: that's the promise of "favor composition over inheritance".
feedback.incorrect: Composition has no negative impact on testability — quite the opposite, it makes injecting mocks easier.

quiz.question: What relationship does composition typically represent?
options: "has-a"
"is-a"
No relationship at all

quiz.question: Why does composition make unit testing easier?
options: You can easily inject a fake dependency (mock) in place of the real one
It removes the need for tests
It makes the code untestable

quiz.question: The famous advice "favor composition over inheritance" means:
options: Prefer assembling behaviors through composition rather than creating deep, rigid inheritance hierarchies
Never use inheritance, under any circumstances
Composition and inheritance are technically incompatible

quiz.question: In which case is inheritance still relevant?
options: When there's a real, stable "is-a" relationship and the hierarchy won't change often
Always, in 100% of cases
Never, inheritance is an anti-pattern

quiz.question: In React, which approach is officially recommended between composition and component inheritance?
options: Composition (components assembled via `children`/props); inheritance between components is discouraged
Systematic inheritance between components
React allows neither

quiz.question: An `Employee extends Person` class adds a salary. A `Manager` also supervises a list of employees. How should this "supervises" relationship be modeled?
options: By composition: the `Manager` has a list of `Employee` (a "has-a" relationship), not by inheritance
By inheritance: `Manager extends Employee[]`
It doesn't matter, inheritance and composition are interchangeable here

quiz.question: Why does composition make classic `instanceof`-based polymorphism trickier?
options: A composed object doesn't inherit the type of its internal dependencies: `object instanceof FlyBehavior` will be false even if the behavior is injected
It doesn't make it harder, it's strictly equivalent to inheritance
Composition completely forbids polymorphism

culture: React strongly popularized composition in frontend culture: components are assembled via children/props rather than through class inheritance, which has gotten a whole generation of web developers used to thinking "composition" by default.

pionnier.nom: Erich Gamma and the Gang of Four co-authors
pionnier.portrait: Erich Gamma, a Swiss computer scientist, along with Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, and John Vlissides, co-wrote the book "Design Patterns", published in 1994.
pionnier.contribution: They catalogued and formalized 23 object-oriented design patterns, including the principle "favor composition over inheritance".
pionnier.problematique: Deep inheritance hierarchies made code fragile: modifying a parent class had unpredictable side effects on all its child classes, and behavior fixed at compile time lacked flexibility.
pionnier.solution: Build behaviors by assembling objects together (a "has-a" relationship) rather than stacking layers of inheritance (an "is-a" relationship), so behavior could be changed at runtime.
pionnier.resultat: This principle has become an almost universal reference in software design and directly influenced the design of modern APIs, including React's Hooks.

ambiguite.question: Is using React Hooks (useEffect, useState) a form of composition?
ambiguite.reponse: Yes, in spirit: Hooks let you compose reusable behaviors into a component without inheriting from a base class — a direct application of the "composition over inheritance" principle.

title: Functional programming vs object-oriented programming
griotIntro: Two griots can tell the same story differently: one by describing characters who evolve, the other by chaining pure transformations, never changing the past.
OOP organizes code around objects with state; functional programming favors pure functions and immutability.

explanation.text: A pure function always returns the same result for the same inputs, with no side effects — immutability is one of its pillars, widely used by React and Redux. Click on the lines to see the difference.

annotations.note: `push` modifies the original `arr` array IN PLACE — any other code holding a reference to that same array sees the change, even without asking for it.
`[...arr, x]` creates a brand new array — the original `arr` is never touched. Same input → always the same result, with no side effects.
The spread `[...list]` only copies the first level (a shallow copy) — the objects it contains remain the same references.
`copy[0].name = 'modified'` therefore mutates the original `list[0]` object despite looking like a "pure" function — a classic interview trap about immutability.

useCases: This project's `useProgress` hook updates XP with `{ ...prev, xp: prev.xp + amount }`, never mutating the previous object — a classic React pattern.
JavaScript's `.map()`, `.filter()`, `.reduce()` functions, widely used to transform data lists without imperative loops.
Redux or Zustand, which require pure reducers to keep state predictable and debuggable via tools like Redux DevTools.

relatedTools.name: Redux / Redux Toolkit
relatedTools.description: Enforces pure reducers and immutable state, at the heart of functional programming applied to state management.

relatedTools.name: Ramda / Lodash/fp
relatedTools.description: JavaScript libraries dedicated to functional programming (composition, currying, immutability).

relatedTools.name: Elixir / Haskell / Clojure
relatedTools.description: "Purely" functional languages by design, good examples for understanding the paradigm in depth.

bugHunt.explanation: `applyDiscount` directly mutates each `item.price` of the original array passed as a parameter — a hidden side effect: any calling code holding a reference to `items` sees its prices change without having asked for it. A pure functional version would return a new array with new objects: `items.map(item => ({ ...item, price: item.price * (1 - percentage) }))`.

practice.question: What is a pure function?
options: A function that always returns the same result for the same inputs, with no side effects (no external mutation, no I/O)
A function with no parameters
A function that always modifies a global variable

feedback.correct: Correct — predictability and the absence of side effects are the two key criteria of a pure function.
feedback.incorrect: A pure function is defined by its predictability and lack of side effects, not by its number of parameters.

quiz.question: Why does immutability make debugging easier in a large application?
options: Data never changes "under your feet" elsewhere in the code, which reduces unexpected side effects
It makes the code harder to understand
It has nothing to do with debugging

quiz.question: In React, why should you never mutate state directly (e.g. `state.push(x)`)?
options: React compares references to detect changes and trigger a re-render; mutating directly breaks this detection
It technically has no consequence
React forbids any kind of array in state

quiz.question: What is a higher-order function?
options: A function that takes another function as a parameter and/or returns a function (e.g. `map`, `filter`)
A function defined at the very top of a file
A function that never returns anything

quiz.question: Are OOP and functional programming incompatible within the same language?
options: No — JavaScript, for example, allows mixing both paradigms as needed
Yes, you must pick a single paradigm for the whole project
Yes, they are completely separate kinds of languages

quiz.question: What is one advantage of pure functions for unit testing?
options: No need to mock anything: same inputs, same outputs, always
They are impossible to test
They always require a database to be tested

quiz.question: Why doesn't `const obj = Object.freeze({ profile: { age: 20 } })` guarantee deep immutability?
options: `Object.freeze` is shallow: nested objects like `obj.profile` remain mutable
`Object.freeze` makes absolutely everything immutable, including nested objects
`Object.freeze` has no effect in modern JavaScript

quiz.question: What is the hidden side effect in this code: `function sort(arr) { return arr.sort(); }`?
options: `Array.prototype.sort()` sorts the array IN PLACE and returns the same reference: the function mutates its argument despite looking like a pure function
None, `sort()` always returns a copy of the array
The issue is purely about performance, not the function's purity

culture: Functional programming has made a real comeback in JS culture since the rise of React/Redux (2015+): historically academic concepts (Haskell, Lisp) like immutability have become standard expectations in modern frontend interviews.

pionnier.portrait: American computer scientist, Stanford professor, pioneer of artificial intelligence and creator of the Lisp language in 1958.
pionnier.contribution: He designed Lisp, one of the very first languages to formalize the principles of functional programming (functions as values, recursion, list processing).
pionnier.problematique: Manipulating code and data interchangeably for artificial intelligence research, where programs needed to reason about evolving symbolic structures.
pionnier.solution: Represent both code and data as lists, and treat functions as first-class values that can be passed, combined, and returned by other functions.
pionnier.resultat: Lisp introduced concepts still used today (recursion, garbage collection, higher-order functions) and directly influenced modern functional languages as well as JavaScript practices like `.map()` and `.reduce()`.

ambiguite.question: Is JavaScript a functional or an object-oriented language?
ambiguite.reponse: Strictly neither: JavaScript is multi-paradigm, it allows both styles (ES6 classes for OOP, pure functions for FP) without imposing either one — a style choice left to the developer or the team.
